opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's the question I've been circling for my whole research career, and AMI Labs is the first place where I feel we can attack it head-on, without compromise.

For the last several years, the field has been dominated by one recipe: scale up language models, predict the next token, and hope that intelligence emerges from text. And it's been incredibly successful. I don't want to dismiss that at all. But I've always felt something essential is missing. Language is a very compressed, very human-filtered view of the world. A child learns an enormous amount about physics, objects, cause and effect, and other agents long before they can speak. That kind of understanding comes from perceiving and interacting with the real world, from vision, from action, from building internal models of how things work.

That's really the core of what we mean by world models. A system should be able to observe the world, build an abstract representation of it, predict what will happen, and plan its actions based on that. Not just generate pixels or tokens, but actually understand. I've spent a lot of my time on visual representation learning, on how models see, and over time it became very clear to me that vision isn't just one more modality you bolt onto a language model. It may be the foundation.

So why devote my life to it? Partly because I think it's the right scientific bet, and somebody has to make that bet seriously, with real resources and real conviction, rather than as a side project inside a company whose main business is something else. Partly because of the people. Working with Yann, who has been arguing for this vision for decades, often when it was unpopular, and with a team that shares that long-term view, is very rare.

And honestly, partly because it's hard. If we're right, this is the path toward machines that can reason about the physical world, help in robotics, science, everyday life, in ways current systems can't. If we're wrong, we'll still learn a lot about what intelligence actually requires. Either way, I think it's one of the most important questions of our time, and I'd rather spend my years working on that than on incremental improvements to something that already exists.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts LLM efforts focused on scaling next-token prediction from text with AMI Labs’ focus on learning from perception, interaction, and world models.

r002.rationale: It says AMI Labs is the first place where the guest can pursue this question “head-on, without compromise,” and connects that work to the potential path toward machines that can reason about the physical world.

r003.rationale: The guest says they would rather spend their years on this research even if the team is wrong, because they would still learn what intelligence requires.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question to open with, and honestly, "devoting your life to" is a heavy phrase. But I'll try to answer it truthfully.

For most of my career I've been working on what you might call the perception side of AI. Vision, representation learning, how a model sees the world. And over the last few years, watching language models take off, I've had this persistent feeling that we've built something incredibly impressive but also strangely incomplete. These systems can write beautifully about a cup falling off a table, but they don't really understand what it means for a cup to fall. They don't have a model of the world in the sense that a two-year-old does.

That gap is what drew me to AMI Labs. The core bet there, which I share deeply, is that the next real breakthrough isn't going to come from scaling text prediction further. It's going to come from building systems that learn how the world works from observation and interaction, the way animals and humans do. World models, planning, grounded intelligence. Yann has been saying this for years, sometimes to a lot of pushback, and I think he's fundamentally right about the direction even if nobody knows the exact path yet.

So why devote myself to it? A few reasons.

First, I think this is one of the genuinely open scientific problems left. A lot of what's happening in the industry right now is engineering and productization of ideas that are already understood. That's valuable, but it's not what gets me out of bed. The question of how a system builds an internal model of physical reality from raw sensory data, and uses it to reason and plan, is still wide open. There's real science to do.

Second, the people. Research is a social activity. You want to be around people who disagree with you productively, who push on your assumptions. AMI has that concentration of people who have thought about these problems for a long time and aren't just chasing the current benchmark.

Third, and this is more personal, I've always believed that visual understanding is central to intelligence, not a side quest. For a long time it felt like vision was being treated as a downstream application of language models. At AMI, perception and world modeling are at the center of the agenda, not the periphery. That alignment matters to me.

And I'd add one honest caveat. I don't think any single lab has a monopoly on the right answer. There's a real chance this approach takes much longer than we hope, or that the field finds another route. But if you're going to spend years of your life on something, it should be a problem that's important enough that even partial progress is meaningful. This is one of those. If we get even halfway there, we'll have learned something fundamental about how intelligence works, and that feels worth it to me.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts world modeling with scaling text prediction, but does not clearly say that AMI is broadening its problem scope while many current LLM efforts are narrowing theirs.

r002.rationale: It describes AMI’s focus on world models and grounded intelligence as an open scientific problem with potential for a real breakthrough.

r003.rationale: The speaker says the work is worth devoting years to despite acknowledging that it may take longer than hoped or that the field may find another route.

astra-6.text:
For me, it comes down to a question: what would it take to build intelligence that really understands the world? A system that can observe what’s happening, anticipate the consequences of its actions, and use that understanding to make decisions. That’s the problem I want to spend my time on.

We’ve made tremendous progress in AI, but there are still fundamental questions about how machines learn from experience. How do they learn what matters without someone labeling everything? How do they build an understanding that transfers to a situation they’ve never encountered before? Those questions are what make research exciting to me.

I see AMI Labs as an opportunity to pursue that direction seriously—to connect fundamental research with systems that can do something useful in the world. There’s uncertainty, of course. I wouldn’t say I know exactly how it will work out. But when I think about what would be worth years of effort, this is the kind of problem I keep coming back to.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad goal of building intelligence that understands the world, but does not contrast AMI Labs’ scope with narrower problems in current LLM efforts.

r002.rationale: It says AMI Labs offers an opportunity to pursue the direction seriously, but does not present that scope as creating room for potential breakthroughs.

r003.rationale: The response expresses willingness to spend time and years on the research despite uncertainty, but does not clearly commit a lifetime or mention uncertainty about whether the work will produce a breakthrough.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it comes down to a question: what is still missing from intelligence? We’ve made remarkable progress with systems that learn from language, but there’s still a gap between being able to talk about the world and being able to understand it well enough to act in it.

That’s the problem I want to spend my time on. How do we build systems that learn from what they observe, develop an understanding of how things change, and use that understanding to plan? It connects very naturally to why I became interested in visual intelligence in the first place.

I wouldn’t say you can know in advance that an organization is worth your entire life. But you can find a problem that feels worth decades of effort. For me, this is one of those problems. AMI Labs is an opportunity to commit to it—to take the uncertainty seriously and still try to build something fundamental.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language systems with the ability to understand and act in the world, but does not say AMI Labs deliberately broadens its scope while many LLM efforts narrow theirs.

r002.rationale: It calls the problem fundamental and worth decades of effort, but does not connect a broader scope to room for potential breakthroughs.

r003.rationale: The response expresses commitment despite uncertainty, but leaves that uncertainty unspecified; it does not clearly say the research may or may not yield a breakthrough.
